title: Enhancement of the Topological Hall Effect through Engineering the Skyrmion Size and Shape
authors: Kazuma Murata, Ryunosuke Terasawa, Hiroaki Ishizuka
abstract: The topological Hall effect of skyrmions is a promising electrical probe of magnetic textures, but its small magnitude limits applications. In this work, we theoretically investigate the topological Hall effect induced by sparsely distributed skyrmions in the weak-coupling limit, focusing on how the size and shape of the skyrmion affect the Hall effect. To this end, we used a formalism based on angular-momentum eigenstates, which enables systematic analysis within reasonable computation time. We found that, in clean materials where the electron mean-free path is comparable to or larger than the skyrmion size, the Hall effect depends considerably on the size and shape of the skyrmion. In particular, the Hall effect is largest when $k_Fλ\sim 1$, and its magnitude can be tuned by the domain-wall width of skyrmions. These findings provide a basis for investigating how the shape and size of skyrmions affect transport properties and demonstrate that the topological Hall effect is controllable by engineering these properties.
summary: This theoretical work investigates the topological Hall effect generated by skyrmions, demonstrating that the effect is highly tunable by controlling the skyrmion's physical dimensions (size and shape). By analyzing the conductivity in the weak-coupling limit, the authors predict an optimal condition for maximum THE when $k_F\lambda \sim 1$. These findings establish a pathway for engineering magnetic materials to control charge transport via magnetic texture engineering.
main_problem: The study investigates how the topological Hall effect (THE) induced by sparsely distributed magnetic skyrmions can be enhanced and controlled by engineering the skyrmion's size and shape.
main_result: The THE is found to depend significantly on the skyrmion size and shape, exhibiting a peak when the Fermi wave vector times the skyrmion size ($k_F\lambda$) is near unity, and its magnitude can be tuned by the domain-wall width.
method: The analysis uses a theoretical formalism based on angular-momentum eigenstates and derives the Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$) using the second Born approximation for weak electron-magnon coupling.
model_or_system: The system models electron transport in a 2D itinerant electron gas coupled to localized magnetic moments forming skyrmions. The Hamiltonian describes this coupling, and the skyrmion structure is characterized by a radius ($\lambda$) and domain-wall width ($\xi$).
key_observables: Topological Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$), which is the primary measurable quantity.
important_parameters: Skyrmion size ($\lambda$), domain-wall width ($\xi$), Fermi wave vector ($k_F$), and the dimensionless parameters $k_F\lambda$ and $\xi/\lambda$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed in the weak-coupling limit and assumes clean materials where the electron mean-free path is comparable to or larger than the skyrmion size.
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows the dependence of $\sigma_{xy}$ on $k_F$ and $\xi/\lambda$ for different skyrmion numbers ($q$). Figure 3 illustrates the dependence of $\sigma_{xy}$ on the skyrmion size ($\lambda$) for $q=1$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$) by deriving expressions in different limits: the general case using scattering theory, the large skyrmion limit ($\lambda 	o \infty$), and the small skyrmion limit ($k_F\lambda 	o 0$).
why_interesting: While the core physics is condensed matter magnetism, the detailed theoretical modeling of transport coefficients ($\sigma_{xy}$) based on geometric parameters ($\lambda, \xi$) and their tunability provides a rich framework for understanding how nanoscale magnetic textures dictate electronic properties, which is relevant to quantum transport studies.

The red arrows indi- cate spins at which electrons are scattered, and the gray lines are the trajectories of single- and multiple-spin-scattering paths that give rise to the asymmetric scattering. (b) Radial profile of the out-of-plane spin component n⊥(r) for the skyrmion in Eq. (3).
